questions.explain: Healthy OLTP systems typically show buffer cache hit ratios above 95%, with most well-configured production databases at 98-99%. Ratios significantly below 95% warrant investigation into buffer pool sizing or scan pollution.
options: Above 50%, since disk I/O is fast enough to compensate
Above 80%, matching the plan cache hit ratio target
Above 95%, with most well-configured production databases at 98-99%
Exactly 100%, since any physical read indicates a bug
questions.q: What buffer cache hit ratio indicates a healthy OLTP system, according to the chapter?

questions.explain: SQL Server opens database files with FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING on Windows, bypassing the OS cache for database I/O — the buffer pool is the single tier of database caching, which is why max server memory is the most consequential memory setting.
options: SQL Server opens database files with FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING, bypassing the OS cache — the buffer pool is the only cache tier
SQL Server delegates caching to the OS page cache, so max server memory is irrelevant on Windows
Lock Pages in Memory doubles the effective buffer pool by compressing pages
Large Pages disable the buffer pool entirely in favor of tempdb caching
questions.q: Why does the chapter say max server memory is the most consequential memory setting on SQL Server?

questions.explain: When SQL Server first compiles a stored procedure plan, it uses the actual parameter values at that moment for cardinality estimates and caches the result. Unusual initial values produce a plan that performs poorly for typical values.
options: A plan that is sniffed from the network instead of the buffer pool
A feature that automatically forces parameterization on ad-hoc queries
A compile storm caused by DBCC DROPCLEANBUFFERS in production
A cached plan compiled with unusual initial parameter values that performs poorly for typical values

questions.explain: sys.dm_os_buffer_descriptors shows how many buffer pool pages each database currently holds, revealing where memory is actually going — valuable on shared instances to find which tables consume the most buffer space.
options: sys.dm_exec_cached_plans, which reports buffer pool pages per object
sys.dm_os_buffer_descriptors, which shows buffer pool pages per database
sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states, which tracks log send queues per database
sys.configurations, which breaks down buffer usage by filegroup
questions.q: Which DMV shows how much of the buffer pool each database is consuming?

questions.explain: DBCC FREEPROCCACHE evicts every plan on the instance and causes a compile storm; the chapter prefers targeted fixes like forced parameterization, plan guides, or targeted eviction using the plan handle.
options: DBCC FREEPROCCACHE, because a cold plan cache compiles faster
DBCC DROPCLEANBUFFERS, because it also frees procedure cache
Running DBCC FREEPROCCACHE routinely, since compile storms are harmless
Avoiding DBCC FREEPROCCACHE in favor of targeted eviction by plan handle or forced parameterization
questions.q: When the plan cache is polluted with single-use ad-hoc plans, what is the chapter's recommended approach?
